extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent practitioners, patent applicants, in-house counsel involved in patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Practical strategies and legal exceptions in U.S. patent prosecution for preventing or delaying the issuance of a final Office Action, referencing MPEP 706.07(a) and relevant CFR provisions. Focuses on tactical choices (argument vs amendment), IDS timing, claim additions, and declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: second Office Actions are typically final (MPEP 706.07(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under MPEP 706.07(a), any second or subsequent Office Action on the merits will be designated as final, unless an exception applies. Once final, an applicant has limited options: they can appeal, file an RCE, or submit an after-final amendment that the examiner may—but is not obligated to—consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that finality is the default for second/subsequent on-the-merits actions; plan prosecution choices (amend vs argue, IDS timing, claim additions) with that default in mind because it limits follow-on remedies and increases costs (appeal or RCE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — examiner introduces a new ground of rejection (must be non-final)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner introduces a new rejection that is not directly necessitated by the applicant’s claim amendments, the Office Action must remain non-final. This ensures fairness by allowing the applicant an opportunity to respond to new reasoning before facing a final rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the article: first OA rejects under §102 based on Reference A; applicant argues without amending; examiner issues a second OA rejecting under §103 using new references B+C — because the new rejection was not caused by claim amendments, the second action must be non-final. Strategic tip: if an examiner is likely to introduce a new rejection based on prior art not previously cited, consider arguing without amending to provoke a shift and avoid finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — new rejection based on an IDS submitted during the permitted timeframe (37 CFR 1.97(c); 1.17(p))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant submits an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) during a specific timeframe and pays the required fee, any subsequent rejection that relies on the newly cited references must be non-final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: examiner initially rejects under §103 based on References A+B; applicant files an IDS with Reference C; examiner cites C in a new rejection. Because the rejection relies on the applicant’s IDS submission, the examiner cannot issue a final rejection. Strategic tip: if you foresee a final rejection, strategically submit an IDS with relevant prior art (and meet timing/fee rules) to force a second non-final Office Action and extend prosecution without an RCE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — argue without amending to provoke a non-final second action
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to respond by argument only (not amending claims) can sometimes cause the examiner to introduce a new ground of rejection in the next action, which by rule must be non-final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tactic when the examiner is likely to rely on additional prior art or new reasoning instead of simply reasserting the original rejection. Risk: if the examiner does not introduce a new ground, you may still receive a final rejection with limited options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — submit an IDS before final rejection to force non-finality
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely submitting an IDS (and paying any required fee) can make any subsequent rejection that relies on those newly cited references non-final under the cited CFR provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a tactical way to extend prosecution without filing an RCE. Ensure the IDS is submitted within the permitted timeframe (per 37 CFR 1.97(c), 1.17(p)) and that the references are relevant; improper or late IDS filings may not produce the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — introduce new claims to reset prosecution (but avoid new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding new claims can be a tactical way to reset prosecution if the new claims introduce significant limitations that require fresh examination and are fully supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements/cautions: the new claim scope must be fully supported by the specification to avoid a new matter rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112(a). This strategy works best when the added claims are substantively different (significant limitations) so the examiner is likely to raise a new ground of rejection; minor variations may not prevent a final Office Action. Not guaranteed — if changes are minor, examiner may still issue final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inventor declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 to strengthen enablement (but not introduce new subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor’s declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 can help establish that a person skilled in the art would understand how to implement a claimed feature, thereby strengthening the record on enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations can clarify how existing features are enabled but cannot introduce new subject matter. Use declarations to address perceived enablement deficiencies, but ensure the content stays within what the specification already discloses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical takeaways: preferred tactical options to keep prosecution open
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarized actionable tactics: (1) argue without amending if the examiner may introduce a new ground of rejection; (2) submit an IDS with relevant prior art before final rejection under 37 CFR 1.97(c) to trigger a non-final action; (3) introduce a new claim that is supported by the specification but forces new examination; (4) use declarations to clarify enablement but ensure they do not introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are complementary tactics — choose based on case circumstances, timing, and risk tolerance. Always confirm procedural compliance (timing, fees, and support) and consider specialist advice for specific cases.
